entities.name: Abel of Reims
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abel of Reims (died 751) was an Anglo-Saxon bishop who served as Archbishop of Reims in the Frankish Church, one of the most important ecclesiastical appointments in the Carolingian realm. Born in England, he was part of the wave of Anglo-Saxon missionaries and clergy who brought Northumbrian and Irish Christian learning to the European continent in the seventh and eighth centuries — a movement that included figures like Willibrord, Boniface, and Alcuin.

Abel's appointment to Reims was part of the broader Anglo-Saxon contribution to Carolingian ecclesiastical reform. He appears in the records of church councils and his tenure is associated with attempts to address the laxity and irregularities in the Frankish Church that reformers like Boniface were simultaneously targeting. His foreign origin — unusual for a Frankish see of Reims's prestige — reflects the trust placed in Anglo-Saxon clergy by both the papacy and the Carolingian rulers.

Reims was one of the most politically significant sees in the Frankish Church: it was the metropolitan see of the northern Frankish realm, closely associated with royal anointing and Carolingian religious legitimacy. An Anglo-Saxon archbishop at Reims indicates the degree to which insular learning and reform traditions had penetrated to the heart of Frankish ecclesiastical culture by the mid-eighth century.
